en: The Sutra on the Poor Old Man Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huìjiǎn.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...

Accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas and ten thousand bodhisattvas, at that time an immeasurable great assembly of devas, nāgas, and spirits gathered together. They respectfully surrounded him, and upon hearing the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, there was none among them who did not rejoice.

At that time, there was an impoverished old man, two hundred years of age, whose eyebrows grew with fine hair, whose ears protruded from his head, and whose teeth were as white as even shells; his hands reached past his knees, and when one looked at his countenance, he appeared to possess the marks of a noble person.

Yet he was so poor and distressed that his clothes did not cover his body; his five limbs were bare, his belly was perpetually empty from hunger, and he could only move with great difficulty, barely maintaining the breath of life.

Hearing that the Buddha was still in the world, his heart was filled with singular joy; day and night he made vows, and after ten years since their inception, he has now finally attained the fruit. Supporting himself on a staff, he came seeking to see the Buddha, but Śakra and Brahmā were attending the gate and commanded that he not be admitted.
Her husband called out loudly, saying:
"I have been unfortunate throughout my life; impoverished and suffering, starving and freezing, I cannot find death, yet I have no reliance for living."

I have heard that the World-Honored One’s benevolence and compassion reach everywhere; all things rely upon you, and there are none who do not receive your grace. My heart was filled with singular joy, and for ten years I have made vows day and night. Only now have I attained the fruit; therefore, I have come from afar to beg for a private audience, seeking liberation from all suffering.
"But you have now cut me off; since this both violates my own wish and contradicts the intention of the Sage, how could it be appropriate?
The Buddha, already knowing this, looked toward Ānanda and said:
"Do you see that elderly, long-lived man with the marks of an old man, whose karmic offenses are not yet exhausted?"
Ānanda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and said to the Buddha:
"How can there be the merit of a venerable elder who yet possesses the *āpatti* (offense)? How could one who has committed an offense possess the [Buddha-]marks?"
"I have never seen such a thing before; where is it now?
The Buddha said, "It is nearby, outside the gate."
“Śakra and Brahmā shall sever this; you may call him forward.

Thereupon, the old man crawled forward on his elbows. Upon seeing the Buddha, he was overcome with a mixture of grief and joy, his tears flowing freely as he prostrated before him. Kneeling for a long time with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have been unfortunate in this life, suffering from poverty and toil, hunger and cold. I seek death but cannot find it, and though I live, I have nothing to rely upon.”

I have heard that the World-Honored One’s benevolence and compassion reach everywhere; all things rely upon him and none fail to receive his grace. My heart is filled with singular joy, and day and night I resolve to bring myself before his countenance.
"I have been here for ten years now, yet only today have I attained the fruit. Previously, I stood outside the gate for a long time without being able to advance.
I calculated that I wished to return, but my strength was insufficient; I had no way to move either forward or back."
I only fear that my life will end here, defiling the holy gate and further increasing my transgressions.
I did not realize that the Celestial Honored One had already taken pity on me and permitted me to advance; to die thus, I shall have no more regrets!
"I only wish to quickly bring my offenses to an end; in future lives, I pray that you will bestow your grace upon me and grant me supreme wisdom.

The Buddha said, "Regarding the causes and conditions of human birth and death, one brings about the roots of offense through manifold causes and conditions. Now, for your sake, I shall explain their fundamental source."

"In your previous life, you were born into the family of a wise and noble king of a powerful great nation; at that time, as a crown prince, your status was extraordinary and your pride was beyond compare. Cherished above by your parents and revered below by your ministers and subjects, you used this position to act according to your own whims, treating others with contempt."

With haughty eyes and a grand gaze, he stands aloof and self-important—yet his vast wealth of billions consists entirely of the people's property, and the poverty of the common folk is caused solely by his tax collection; he knows only how to amass hoards, not how to practice charity.

"At that time, there was a poor and humble śramaṇa named Jingzhi who had come from a distant land; he has traveled here specifically to visit you, and his request is not great—he lacks only a Dharma robe."

Yet you were utterly unworthy of receiving him; you treated him with extreme hostility, neither asking for his robe nor giving him food. He sat empty-handed before you, yet when he departed, you would not even let him go.

For seven days and seven nights, you have been without food or drink; with but a faint breath remaining, your life hangs by a thread like a candle about to go out. Yet you see this and rejoice greatly, gathering a crowd to watch it as if it were the ultimate pleasure.
A courtier standing nearby admonished the minister, saying:
"Do not speak thus, Prince!

These śramaṇas are compassionate and reverent; they possess virtue and morality within. They would not feel cold even if frozen, nor hunger even if starved. The reason they come to beg is solely because they wish to cultivate merit!"
“Since I have not bestowed anything upon them, why do you distress and press them so?
I pray that you will send them away; do not bring their guilt upon me. The Prince replied:
"Who is this person? He falsely claims to possess the Way and its Virtue.
Let us try to trouble him slightly, but do not let him die."
"Let him go as he is; there is no need for concern.
He was immediately sent away and driven out of the country.
While still within ten or more li of the national border, he encountered starving bandits who intended to kill and devour him.
The śramaṇa replied, "I am a poor and freezing śramaṇa, emaciated and reduced to skin and bone; my flesh is both putrid and foul-smelling and unfit for consumption.
I shall surely be killed in vain, as I have no use."
The starving bandits said:
"We have been famished and exhausted for many days and eat nothing but earth.
Although you are somewhat thin, you are nonetheless flesh; we will certainly not let you go, so you must simply face death."
Thus they argued back and forth for a long while in great confusion.
When the Prince learned of this, he went to rescue them and said, "I have already been unable to provide them with food and clothing; how could I now allow these starving bandits to kill them?"
When the bandits saw the Prince, they all bowed their heads, confessed their transgressions, and apologized for their crimes, then released the śramaṇa.
"The śramaṇa at that time was none other than the present-day Maitreya Bodhisattva;
the noble and wealthy Prince was none other than you."
That you now suffer the retribution of this poverty is due to your former stinginess and greed;
that you have obtained a long life is because you once saved the life of a śramaṇa.
"The retribution for sins and blessings follows like a shadow follows a form, or an echo responds to a sound.
The old man said to the Buddha, "What has passed is already so; I wish to conclude my affairs here and now."
"I pray that with this remaining life, I may become a śramaṇa and, in all future births, always attend upon the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"Excellent!

At that moment, the old man's hair and beard fell to the ground; Dharma robes spontaneously appeared upon his body. His physical strength became robust, his hearing and sight were sharpened, and he immediately attained superior wisdom and entered the gate of samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In the past, when you were a prince, You did not recognize the principles of benevolence and righteousness;
Arrogant and noble, you gave yourself license, Relying on your status as a great king."
I once thought myself devoid of both sin and merit, believing that by this I could ensure eternal security.
How could I have realized that the cycle of birth and death would bring its retribution upon me today?
Yet, from my transgressions, I have again received grace, and am now able to behold the God among Gods.
Able to shed past transgressions, They enter the Dharma-gate as their lives draw near its end.
Forever free from the mind of stinginess and greed, They long enjoy the roots of wisdom.
Life after life they attend the Buddha’s side, Preserving their longevity for ten thousand kalpas.
Thereupon, the elder bhikṣu, having heard this sūtra with joy, prostrated before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked toward Ānanda and said:
"If there are those who recite this sūtra, they shall behold the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa."
Those who practice this sutra and cause it to be proclaimed in future generations shall receive a prophecy from Maitreya Buddha.
What the Tathāgata speaks with his broad and long tongue is without any discrepancy.
When the entire great assembly had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they received and upheld it with joy and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on the Poor Old Man Spoken by the Buddha.
